01The Story

In 1992, Adam “Mizda Sandman” Smith got the idea while watching Video Jukebox — a pay-per-video channel where you picked a video and paid for it on your phone bill — with Les “Big” Biglow. A Scarface video, “A Minute to Pray, A Second to Die,” about death in the Black community, struck them as incredibly cool — and they had never seen it before. Then they noticed videos like “Shake That Ass Baby” by Florida group The Dogs and “Me So Horny” by 2 Live Crew playing over and over, sometimes back to back. That is when Adam realized there was a wealth of artists and videos that would never air on MTV or BET — and that someone should start a show playing the clips and supporting the artists that others would not. Hence the birth of the Underground.

Hence the birth of the Underground.Adam “Mizda Sandman” Smith

It was Adam’s idea — but as he puts it, it doesn’t get executed without Les Biglow. Created by Adam Smith and Les “Big” Biglow, the two brought the show to air alongside producer Maria Farris, and what they built — airing Mondays at 11 PM on PCTV 21 — was something television had never seen: an uncensored, R-rated hip-hop video magazine. (Years later, BET would air Uncut, a similar uncensored late-night format — Adam notes the resemblance.)

For 17 years and 333 episodes, Underground Hip-Hop Video Magazine gave the underground a national-grade spotlight — raw interviews, videos, and moments with artists long before and long after the mainstream caught on. The show earned a Billboard Music Awards nomination, a nod from Vibe magazine, and a place in the American Archive of Public Broadcasting.

This page is the start of the show's permanent digital home — built from Adam's personal archive.

07Recognition
  • Billboard Music Awards — nomination for the show.
  • Vibe magazine (1994) — recognized the show as Pittsburgh's essential hip-hop television.
  • The Source — featured in Issue #63 (December 1994), the Scarface-cover issue.
  • Badass TV (UK) — the U.K. hip-hop TV show hosted by Ice-T sent a production crew to Pittsburgh to film a segment on U.H.H.V.M.; it aired in the U.K. and Northern Ireland. (Watch the segment on YouTube)
  • WQED OnQ / American Archive of Public Broadcasting — Adam Smith featured as community contributor; footage preserved in the national archive.
  • Carnegie Mellon Hip-Hop Arts Greenhouse — Adam Smith guest speaker on panel.
  • Rap Sheet conference — Adam Smith served as moderator for a hip-hop panel at a conference held by the publication Rap Sheet (founded by Darryl James).
Gold & Platinum — presented to U.H.H.V.M. for supporting the artists and the culture
